monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: cache.t4g.medium — AWS ElastiCache us-east-1 / On-Demand / Redis engine / standard support / 730 h per month; node-hour only. Band: zero-width at the Redis/Memcached standard-support rate. The Valkey engine is CHEAPER and Extended Support is DEARER; both are different products/support states, not a price range for this row, so they are named here rather than used as band edges.

db.m6i.large — AWS RDS PostgreSQL us-east-1 / On-Demand / Single-AZ (band high = Multi-AZ) / 730 h per month; INSTANCE-HOURS ONLY (excludes storage, provisioned IOPS and backup above the free allocation). Band: deployment spread: low = Single-AZ, high = Multi-AZ. Both are on-demand, standard-tier, us-east-1 PostgreSQL, so the band is fully in scope. Multi-AZ is ~2x Single-AZ.

citations.note: $0.178/h Single-AZ x 730 = 12994c/month. MySQL/MariaDB run ~3.9% cheaper than PostgreSQL for the same class.

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 15,000 ops/s at peak (a Friday dinner rush), counted across all flows. Only ~900/s are actual orders: 65% of the traffic is courier GPS pings and customers watching the map, which is the thing people underestimate about this product.

assumptions.subject: track
assumptions.statement: Couriers ping roughly every 4 s while on a job and customers poll every 5 s while waiting. Both go to Redis, not to PostgreSQL — persisting every GPS point to the database is the classic way this design falls over.

assumptions.subject: dispatch
assumptions.statement: Assignment is expensive (~40 ms: geo query over available couriers, then a scoring pass), so each instance handles only ~350 assignments/s. It runs off the event bus rather than in the customer's request path, so a slow match delays the courier, not the checkout.

assumptions.subject: search
assumptions.statement: Discovery is the heaviest read path (~25 ms per query: geo filter, ranking, availability), which is why search carries more instances than the order service despite lower traffic than tracking.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: Real-time map streaming to the customer app is modelled as POLLING, because streaming/push is outside Keystone v1 scope. A WebSocket implementation would move that load from request rate to concurrent connections and change the tracking tier's sizing.

assumptions.subject: search-headroom
assumptions.statement: Discovery is held near 62% utilisation rather than the 85% ceiling: at 85% the same 25 ms query would sit ~167 ms in queue, and search latency is what customers experience as the app being slow.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: Single PostgreSQL primary for orders and reference data — a single point of failure. Menus and courier positions are cached, so it only sees ~2,200 rps of the 15,000.

_library.summary: Ordering, courier dispatch and live delivery tracking for a food-delivery marketplace.
